outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 changes the known bounds on the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane, which Wikipedia (last edited 7 Oct 2026), MathWorld (updated 2 Oct 2026) and Erdős Problem #508 (edited 22 Jan 2026) still give as 5 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7; the in-window activity is on variants (a six-colouring problem with a second forbidden distance, an interval-of-distances problem, the independence ratio and fractional chromatic number), on a Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic graph that leaves the bound at 5, and on neighbouring problems (the density of unit-distance-free sets, the Erdős unit-distance count).
problem_asks: (1) The exact value of χ(ℝ²): the least number of colours needed to colour every point of the Euclidean plane so that no two points at distance 1 share a colour. Known: 5 ≤ χ ≤ 7, so the open question is which of 5, 6, 7 it is. (2) Equivalently (de Bruijn–Erdős, under choice), the largest chromatic number of a finite unit-distance graph in the plane, so the question also asks for lower bounds from finite graphs and upper bounds by colourings of the whole plane. (3) The bullet's own framing is 'the chromatic number of unit distance graphs'; the statement asks only about the single forbidden distance 1, not about other distances, intervals of distances, dimensions other than 2, or fractional or density versions.

events.what_happened: John R. Isbell observed that congruent regular hexagons tiling the plane can be given seven colours so that same-coloured tiles are more than a diameter apart, giving χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7. Source for the attribution and year is the Wikipedia article and MathWorld, both fetched; the 1950 date is as given by those pages (Soifer 2008 is cited there), not from a primary paper.
events.delivers: χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7 for the single-distance problem, the standing upper bound.
events.remains: Whether 5, 6 or 7 is the exact value (lower bound 5 came later, see de Grey 2018).
events.directly_checkable: Yes: the hexagonal tiling and its seven-colouring can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Upper-bound side; cuts toward χ ≤ 7 (no change since).
events.object: The hexagonal tiling of the plane by congruent regular hexagons, with a seven-colouring in which same-coloured hexagons are separated by more than their diameter; explicit.

events.what_happened: Aubrey de Grey, 'The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5', arXiv 1804.02385. Abstract (fetched; the page limits quotes): 'We present a family of finite unit-distance graphs in the plane that are not 4-colourable.' Smallest such graph reported at 1581 vertices in secondary sources (Polymath16 and MathWorld summaries); the full text was not read. This is the event that raised the lower bound from 4 to 5 and started Polymath16 (launched April 2018 by Dustin Mixon and Aubrey de Grey, declared victory 1 Feb 2021 per the Wikipedia references).
events.revisions: v2 11 Apr 2018; v3 30 May 2018 (the version shown on the arXiv page).
events.delivers: χ(ℝ²) ≥ 5, for the single-distance problem as stated. The witnesses are finite unit-distance graphs that are not 4-colourable; no restriction on the problem.
events.remains: Exact value of χ(ℝ²) (5, 6 or 7); upper bound 7 untouched.

checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote an alternate proof of the 'at least 5' fact, which is a reading of the argument rather than a verification of de Grey's graph.

events.directly_checkable: The 1581-vertex graph is not hand-checkable; the non-4-colourability is computer-assisted per secondary sources. Smaller 5-chromatic witnesses (Heule, Parts) were produced from it and are SAT-certified.
events.direction: Lower-bound side: raises χ(ℝ²) ≥ 4 to χ(ℝ²) ≥ 5.
events.object: A family of finite unit-distance graphs in the plane that are not 4-colourable, built from copies of the Moser spindle and related pieces, the smallest reported at 1581 vertices. Explicit coordinates; non-4-colourability established by a computer-assisted case analysis (per secondary sources).

events.what_happened: Jaan Parts, 'On the plane and its coloring', arXiv 2206.12633; Geombinatorics 31/4 (2022) 189-195. Abstract (fetched verbatim): 'We provide a human-verifiable proof that, in a certain sense, the chromatic number of the plane is exactly 7.' The HTML text (ar5iv and arXiv HTML, fetched; summary not verbatim) says the 'certain sense' is a forbidden-distance interval 1 ≤ f ≤ d with d in (2·sin(2π/9), √7/2], not a single distance. Lower bound: a 19-vertex graph (an 18-vertex ring of points on a unit circle plus a centre joined to all of them), with 7 colours forced by a hand case analysis. Upper bound: Isbell's hexagonal tiling. The text claims no computer use.
events.delivers: For the interval-of-forbidden-distances variant (distances from 1 to d, d in (2·sin(2π/9), √7/2]), the chromatic number is 7. Restriction: the forbidden set is an interval containing 1 and reaching d, not the single distance 1 that the problem states.
events.remains: The problem as stated (only distance 1 forbidden): still 5 ≤ χ ≤ 7 per Wikipedia (7 Oct 2026) and MathWorld (2 Oct 2026).

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the paper.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, 2022 (per the arXiv journal reference; the refereeing was not read).

events.directly_checkable: The 19-vertex graph is hand-checkable per the paper's approach (per the HTML summary).
events.doubts: (a) The abstract states 'exactly 7' without its scope; read alone it looks like a resolution of the problem. The scope in the text is the interval variant. (b) Neither Wikipedia (7 Oct 2026) nor MathWorld (2 Oct 2026) mentions it, nor Erdős #508 (edited 22 Jan 2026). (c) The fetched text opens with an unusual introduction about 'the rainbow contains seven colors', a register noted without weighing it. (d) Journal refereeing was not read.
events.direction: Cuts toward χ = 7 for the interval variant (a lower bound of 7 for forbidden-distance intervals). On the single-distance problem it is silent: the upper bound 7 is already known and the lower bound stays at 5.
events.object: A 19-vertex planar graph: an 18-vertex ring of points on a unit circle, plus a central vertex joined to every ring vertex, with edge lengths 1 and 2·sin(2π/9). The ring needs 4 colours by a hand case analysis, and the centre adds 3 more, giving 7 (per the HTML summary of the argument). Explicit and hand-checkable.

events.what_happened: Gergely Ambrus, Adrián Csiszárik, Máté Matolcsi, Dániel Varga and Pál Zsámboki, 'The density of planar sets avoiding unit distances', arXiv 2207.14179. Abstract (fetched): 'we prove a conjecture of Erdős that the density of any measurable planar set avoiding unit distances cannot exceed 1/4'; 'Our argument implies the upper bound of 0.2470.' Version history: v2 20 Oct 2022; v3 28 Jul 2023 ('to appear in Mathematical Programming'). Dániel Varga's institute post of 10 Dec 2023 (fetched) describes the method as 'computer search' with 'a modified beam search' on a cluster that found 'a 23-point configuration suitable for proving the conjecture', and says 'we are in the process of employing a transformer-based machine learning model to guide the computer search'. An institute announcement (undated; ©2024 footer) describes the work as done 'using artificial intelligence methods'.
events.revisions: v2 20 Oct 2022; v3 28 Jul 2023 (final version, 'to appear in Mathematical Programming').
events.delivers: A bound on the density of a measurable planar set with no two points at unit distance (≤ 1/4, in fact ≤ 0.2470). Restriction: measurable sets and density, not a colour count. This is Erdős's density question, a neighbouring problem.
events.remains: The chromatic number of the plane is untouched; the exact density is not settled by this event.

events.what_happened: Konrad Mundinger, Sebastian Pokutta, Christoph Spiegel and Max Zimmer, 'Extending the Continuum of Six-Colorings', arXiv 2404.05509 (single version). Abstract (fetched; summary, the page limits quotes): two novel six-colourings of the Euclidean plane, in which five colours avoid monochromatic unit-distance pairs and the sixth avoids monochromatic pairs at a specified distance d; the range of d is extended to 0.354 ≤ d ≤ 0.657, described as 'the first improvement in 30 years'. The constructions are 'derived by formalizing colorings suggested by a custom machine learning approach'.

It does not give a six-colouring in which every colour class avoids unit distance, so it does not bound χ(ℝ²) ≤ 6.

events.object: Two explicit six-colourings of the Euclidean plane: five classes avoid unit distance, one class avoids distance d for d in [0.354, 0.657] (per the abstract summary).

events.what_happened: Ákos Dúcz and Dániel Varga, 'A unit-distance graph in the plane with independence ratio below 1/4', arXiv 2606.28157 (v1 only, 26 Jun 2026). Abstract (fetched HTML, v1): 'We prove that there exists a finite unit-distance graph in the plane with independence ratio strictly smaller than 1/4.' Theorem 1 states α(G)/|V(G)| < 1/4. Erdős Problem #1070 forum thread (fetched): the second part of #1070 is answered negatively; the first part (estimating f(n)) is open. The result disproves the conjecture of Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga and Zsámboki that the limit is 1/4 (per the abstract as summarised). The authors' declaration on AI use, quoted in the HTML: 'The authors used OpenAI's ChatGPT (GPT-5.5) during the preparation of this manuscript for language editing' and 'Codex was asked to help search for vertices of the optimal primal face of a linear program'.
events.delivers: A finite unit-distance graph in the plane with independence ratio below 1/4, from which the fractional chromatic number of the plane is above 4 (per the abstract). Restriction: a statement about independence ratio (and so the fractional chromatic number), not the chromatic number. Since χ ≥ χ_f, the implied bound χ > 4 is already implied by the known χ ≥ 5.
events.remains: χ(ℝ²) ∈ {5, 6, 7}, and the first part of Erdős #1070.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib4 (Lean v4.32.0-rc1), formalisation of Theorem 1 by Beatrix Benkő (see separate event)

events.directly_checkable: The graph is an existence result; the construction is not explicit in the sense of a short list of coordinates, and the graph is described as astronomically large (abstract, and MathWorld summary, not opened).
events.doubts: (a) Not peer reviewed; MathWorld reports no independent peer review as of 21 Sep 2026 (search summary). (b) An existence argument with an enormous graph; the verifying Lean check depends on roughly 500,000 linear inequalities (forum comment) and on 13 native_decide axioms (README), which rely on the compiler's evaluation beyond the kernel. (c) The MRVZ paper it builds on is itself still under peer review (forum comment). (d) The Erdős forum notes disagreement about how to read the two-part question (StijnC, 29 Jun 2026), so whether #1070 is 'resolved' is contested.
events.direction: Cuts against the conjectured value 1/4 for the independence-ratio question (Erdős #1070). It has no direction for χ(ℝ²).
events.object: A finite planar unit-distance graph with α/|V| < 1/4. The existence proof uses blow-up operations applied to the geometric fractional colouring data of a 29-vertex 'snail' graph (independence ratio 15/29), per the MathWorld summary (not opened). The vertex count is described as astronomically large.

events.what_happened: Jan Kristian Haugland, 'A Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices in the plane', arXiv 2608.04542 (single author). v1 5 Aug 2026; v2 6 Aug; v3 10 Aug; v4 17 Aug; v5 6 Oct 2026. Abstract (fetched summary): a 5-chromatic unit-distance graph on 2131 vertices with no Moser spindle, built from a 21-vertex 7-fold symmetric unit-distance graph by its arcs; the author says it is 'not a record small result'. Method (HTML, fetched): G1 (740 vertices, 3985 edges) is shown non-4-colourable with the CaDiCaL SAT solver with two specified points forced to share a colour; G3 is argued non-4-colourable by hand from G1; a SAT solver finds a 5-colouring of G3. Comments on the abs page (fetched): 'Added AI use declaration' (v5), 'Added links to preprints with recent developments' and 'Corrected page numbers in one reference'. The AI use declaration (HTML, fetched, verbatim): 'Google's Gemini was used for installing and running SAT solvers, and for some language editing.'

events.what_happened: One manuscript, “The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable” (dated September 23, 2026), claims that every colouring of the Euclidean plane with five colours has a monochromatic unit-distance pair, with no regularity assumption on the colour classes. Its main theorem (thm:main) states that the plane has no proper five-colouring even when arbitrary colour classes are allowed, and so 6 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7. The upper bound 7 is the classical hexagonal colouring (Hadwiger 1961), which the paper reproduces; the new content is the lower bound 6. The argument has two parts. (1) Transfer (thm:transfer, with Proposition palettes-forward and a density-point converse): for every positive integer k, a proper k-colouring of the plane exists if and only if a “weak measurable” k-colouring exists. A weak measurable colouring is a Lebesgue-measurable colouring in which same-coloured unit pairs have zero measure in the product of plane Lebesgue measure and normalised arc length on the circle. The forward direction averages a proper colouring over the algebraic plane, projects onto the continuous factor by conditional expectation, and uses a rigidity theorem (thm:rigidity: every K-invariant probability on the character group with zero mass on the ordinary continuous characters is Haar). The converse uses density points and de Bruijn–Erdős compactness. (2) Theorem weak-five (no weak measurable five-colouring): the paper builds angular palettes at each centre with at most two labels (prop:palette-size), shows that the centres whose transition graph contains a cycle form a locally finite set (thm:cyclic-local-finiteness), extracts a label cycle of length 3, 4 or 5 with compact connected exclusion sets (prop:interface-cycle), and excludes each cycle length by an angular argument (prop:angular-five, prop:angular-four, prop:angular-three). The three-cycle case uses a rational placement certificate for seven points forming a Moser-spindle-type configuration (lem:angular-certificate). A corollary (cor:positive-badness) also states, as a consequence, that a finite unit-distance graph is not five-colourable, with an existential positive constant for the monochromatic-pair frequency.
events.delivers: For the list's problem, the claim establishes the lower bound χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6: there is no proper five-colouring of the plane, with arbitrary colour classes, in ZFC. Together with the known seven-colouring it gives 6 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7, which moves the lower bound from the known 5 to 6. This is the list's part (1). For part (2), the claim gives only an existential finite statement: by de Bruijn–Erdős compactness there is a finite unit-distance graph that is not five-colourable, so its chromatic number is at least 6. The paper does not display this graph, and gives no size or explicit construction. The paper's statement of the problem matches the list's: the plane, distance exactly one, no regularity on the colour classes. The paper does not claim to settle the problem. Its introduction says the alternatives six and seven remain unresolved. Part (3) of the list's problem statement, covering other distances, dimensions other than two, and fractional or density versions, is not addressed.
events.remains: If the claim is correct, χ(ℝ²) is either 6 or 7, and which one holds is open. The paper's footnote mentions a May 14, 2026 manuscript of Reed that claims χ(ℝ²) = 7. The paper says that manuscript's displayed theorem assumes the key density bound as a hypothesis, so it does not establish 7; this is context, not part of this family's claim. Also open: whether six colours suffice (a 6-colouring of the plane would be needed for the lower bound to be sharp), an explicit finite unit-distance graph with chromatic number at least 6 (the paper's graph is existential and of unknown size), and the list's variants with other distances, other dimensions, or fractional and density versions.

machine_checked.scope: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks for the fewest colors needed to color the plane so that points at distance one have different colors. The formalized results prove that five colors do not suffice and that seven colors do suffice. The lower bound applies to arbitrary colorings, with no measurability or continuity assumption; the upper bound includes every boundary point of the coloring regions.

events.doubts: (1) Length and compression: the argument spans about 4,600 lines of LaTeX across eight section files, and the abstract and introduction give only an outline. The interface-cycle construction (prop:interface-cycle) is summarised in an overview paragraph (“A planar cover obstruction forces a nontrivial loop…”), and the caption of its exclusion figure calls the shape “schematic”. I read that proposition's statement and the start of its section only. (2) The seven-point certificate (lem:angular-certificate) is verified by tables of decimal coordinate boxes, polynomial bounds and residual numerators, and the text calls this a rational verification. I read that verification but did not recheck its arithmetic. (3) I did not read the relative-singularity and multiple-averages lemmas in rigidity.tex, nor the middle parts of palettes.tex, transitions.tex, interfaces.tex and angular.tex. My account of them rests on the introduction's outline and the statements I did read. (4) The bounds in cor:positive-badness part (ii) are imported from Bourgeat et al. by citation, and the constant δ = 1/m is non-constructive. I found no inconsistency between the abstract and thm:main.; conditional on: The main theorem assumes nothing beyond ZFC. It cites standard results: the abelian spectral theorem and Bochner's theorem, the Følner criterion for amenable groups, Fourier uniqueness, and de Bruijn–Erdős compactness. Corollary cor:positive-badness part (i) depends on Gwyn and Stavrianos 2020 (Lemma 2.10 and Theorem 2.11), and part (ii) depends on Bourgeat, Heinrich, Melotti and Robert 2015 (Theorems 1–2) for its needle-frequency bounds. The paper cites Sokolov–Voronov 2025 and Voronov 2025 as precedents for its interface and strip arguments, not as steps it relies on.
events.direction: proves a lower bound: χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6, improving the known lower bound 5
events.object: None for the lower bound. Non-five-colourability is proved by contradiction. The finite unit-distance graph in cor:positive-badness is obtained by compactness and is not displayed. The seven-colouring in the proof of thm:main (hexagonal, from Hadwiger 1961) is explicit, but it is the known upper bound, not a new object.

disputes.summary: Parts (arXiv 2206.12633) abstract says the chromatic number of the plane is 'exactly 7' 'in a certain sense'. The HTML text says the sense is a forbidden-distance interval 1 ≤ f ≤ d with d in (2·sin(2π/9), √7/2]. Wikipedia (7 Oct 2026) and MathWorld (2 Oct 2026) say the value is 5, 6 or 7 and do not mention the paper. A reader of the abstract alone could take it as a resolution.
Voronov (arXiv 2304.10163) title says the chromatic number of the plane with an interval of forbidden distances is at least 7. The scope is the interval variant and not the single-distance problem.

For spindle-free 5-chromatic graphs: a search-result summary of Haugland's introduction says Heule reduced the bound to 1441 vertices, while MathWorld (2 Oct 2026, via the Hadwiger–Nelson page, and the Haugland graphs entry as summarised) calls the 2131-vertex G3 the smallest known under that restriction. Not resolved from primary text.

The Dúcz–Varga Lean formalisation is credited to Beatrix Benkő by the Erdős forum ('fully autoformalized, thank you Beatrix Benkő!') and to 'Anthropic's Claude models' by the repository README ('developed with the assistance of Anthropic's Claude models'). The split of work is not stated. Both are recorded; the formalisation of an argument the humans have already proved is not AI involvement in the mathematics under §5.4.

summary: Question: what has happened to the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane (Hadwiger–Nelson) since 26 Jan 2024. Answer from the sources opened: nothing has changed the known bounds. Wikipedia's lead (last edited 7 Oct 2026) says the value is unknown and narrowed to 5, 6 or 7; MathWorld (updated 2 Oct 2026) says 5, 6 or 7 and names the 509-vertex Parts graph as the smallest known 5-chromatic planar unit-distance graph; Erdős #508 (edited 22 Jan 2026) gives 5 ≤ χ ≤ 7. The lower bound 5 rests on de Grey (2018), with an alternate argument by Exoo and Ismailescu (May 2018), and the upper bound 7 on Isbell's hexagonal tiling (1950). Every in-window (after 26 Jan 2024) event bearing on this problem's neighbourhood is a variant or a neighbour: (i) two six-colouring papers in which one colour class may contain a second forbidden distance d, from Mundinger, Pokutta, Spiegel and Zimmer (8 Apr 2024) and Mundinger et al. (30 Jan 2025, ICML 2025), the latter described by its authors as an improvement to the 'off-diagonal variant'; (ii) Dúcz and Varga's independence-ratio result (arXiv 2606.28157, 26 Jun 2026), which answers part of Erdős #1070 and gives a fractional, not a chromatic, statement, with a Lean formalisation of Theorem 1 by Beatrix Benkő (12 Jul 2026); (iii) Haugland's Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic graph on 2131 vertices (arXiv 2608.04542, 5 Aug 2026, revised to v5 on 6 Oct 2026), which is a new 5-chromatic witness that leaves the bound of 5 where it was; and (iv) a sphere-variant preprint (8 Oct 2026, not opened). Pre-window events are included as the record requires: the 2018 lower-bound work (de Grey; Exoo–Ismailescu; Heule; Heule 2019 trimming to 529), Parts 2020 (509 vertices; human-verifiable proof of ≥ 5), Voronov et al. 2021 (planar graphs on 64513 vertices with no Moser spindle), Parts 2022 ('exactly 7' for an interval variant), Voronov 2023 (interval variant, χ ≥ 7), Matolcsi et al. 2023 (fractional chromatic number ≥ 4), and de Grey and Parts 2023 (vertex-count bounds). Close calls, on both sides. (a) Parts 2022: the abstract's 'exactly 7' reads as a resolution; the scope in the text is the interval variant, so I record it as a variant result, but the later pass should read the HTML text itself. (b) The AI record: no AI system has been credited with a result on the single-distance problem. The AI contributions in view are: a 'custom machine learning approach' and 'neural networks' in the six-colouring variant (both load-bearing for the variant, both recorded in ai.systems); 'Codex' in the Dúcz–Varga paper, where the declaration says it helped search for vertices of an LP's optimal primal face. That is computational search inside the construction, and I have put it in ai.systems as borderline, because the declaration does not say whether the step was essential. ChatGPT (GPT-5.5) in the same declaration was used for language editing and is not in ai.systems. Gemini in Haugland's declaration was used 'for installing and running SAT solvers, and for some language editing'. Running SAT solvers produced the non-4-colourability certificate for G1, so this is close; I have left Gemini out of ai.systems as tooling (the rule for debugging and running code), and the pass can reverse that. The Benkő Lean formalisation was assisted by 'Anthropic's Claude models', but it formalises a human-proved theorem, so it is not in ai.systems. The OpenAI counterexample (20 May 2026) and the Rényi density result (2022, with a transformer model 'in the process' of guiding search in Dec 2023) are neighbouring problems, recorded as events with the reason they fall outside. (c) Erdős #1070's first part (f(n)) and the second part are not the chromatic number, and the Dúcz–Varga result answers only the second part. (d) The 'exactly 7' and 'at least 7' titles are both interval-variant results; neither the Wikipedia lead nor MathWorld mentions them.
competing_reading: (1) Read Parts 2022 ('the chromatic number of the plane is exactly 7', human-verifiable) at face value: the problem would then be settled at 7, and the 2022 event would be the resolution. Against: the paper's own introduction restricts the claim to interval-of-distances colourings with d in a range, and no later source treats it as a resolution. (2) Read the Mundinger ML six-colourings as AI progress on the problem: the authors call it an improvement to the 'off-diagonal variant', and the colourings allow one colour class a second distance, so they do not give χ(ℝ²) ≤ 6. (3) Count Codex in Dúcz–Varga as load-bearing (LP vertex search inside the construction) or exclude it as computation: the declaration does not say which step. (4) Count Gemini in Haugland as running the SAT certificate, which is part of the non-4-colourability proof of G1, or exclude it as tooling. (5) Read Dúcz–Varga as a resolution of a part of the chromatic-number question: it is not, because it concerns the independence ratio and the fractional chromatic number, and the bound χ ≥ 5 it implies is already known.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full text of Parts 2022 (Geombinatorics 31/4) to confirm the exact scope and the refereeing. (b) Whether Dúcz–Varga's LP search (Codex) produced a step the proof needs, from the authors' text (the arXiv HTML section 7 expanded) or from the authors. (c) Whether Haugland's SAT runs are part of the claimed proof, or only a check; and the Haugland introduction on the 1441 claim. (d) Journal refereeing of Dúcz–Varga and Haugland. (e) The Lean source files of Benkő's repository, and whether the 13 native_decide axioms are acceptable under the pass's standard. (f) An OpenAI primary announcement, which was blocked here. (g) The preprints.org manuscript (Oct 2026), blocked here. (h) Any 2026 source that states a new bound on χ(ℝ²) itself, which none of the searches found.

event.delivers: For the list's problem, the claim establishes the lower bound χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6: there is no proper five-colouring of the plane, with arbitrary colour classes, in ZFC. Together with the known seven-colouring it gives 6 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7, which moves the lower bound from the known 5 to 6. This is the list's part (1). For part (2), the claim gives only an existential finite statement: by de Bruijn–Erdős compactness there is a finite unit-distance graph that is not five-colourable, so its chromatic number is at least 6. The paper does not display this graph, and gives no size or explicit construction. The paper's statement of the problem matches the list's: the plane, distance exactly one, no regularity on the colour classes. The paper does not claim to settle the problem. Its introduction says the alternatives six and seven remain unresolved. Part (3) of the list's problem statement, covering other distances, dimensions other than two, and fractional or density versions, is not addressed.
event.remains: If the claim is correct, χ(ℝ²) is either 6 or 7, and which one holds is open. The paper's footnote mentions a May 14, 2026 manuscript of Reed that claims χ(ℝ²) = 7. The paper says that manuscript's displayed theorem assumes the key density bound as a hypothesis, so it does not establish 7; this is context, not part of this family's claim. Also open: whether six colours suffice (a 6-colouring of the plane would be needed for the lower bound to be sharp), an explicit finite unit-distance graph with chromatic number at least 6 (the paper's graph is existential and of unknown size), and the list's variants with other distances, other dimensions, or fractional and density versions.

machine_checked.scope: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks for the fewest colors needed to color the plane so that points at distance one have different colors. The formalized results prove that five colors do not suffice and that seven colors do suffice. The lower bound applies to arbitrary colorings, with no measurability or continuity assumption; the upper bound includes every boundary point of the coloring regions.

event.doubts: (1) Length and compression: the argument spans about 4,600 lines of LaTeX across eight section files, and the abstract and introduction give only an outline. The interface-cycle construction (prop:interface-cycle) is summarised in an overview paragraph (“A planar cover obstruction forces a nontrivial loop…”), and the caption of its exclusion figure calls the shape “schematic”. I read that proposition's statement and the start of its section only. (2) The seven-point certificate (lem:angular-certificate) is verified by tables of decimal coordinate boxes, polynomial bounds and residual numerators, and the text calls this a rational verification. I read that verification but did not recheck its arithmetic. (3) I did not read the relative-singularity and multiple-averages lemmas in rigidity.tex, nor the middle parts of palettes.tex, transitions.tex, interfaces.tex and angular.tex. My account of them rests on the introduction's outline and the statements I did read. (4) The bounds in cor:positive-badness part (ii) are imported from Bourgeat et al. by citation, and the constant δ = 1/m is non-constructive. I found no inconsistency between the abstract and thm:main.; conditional on: The main theorem assumes nothing beyond ZFC. It cites standard results: the abelian spectral theorem and Bochner's theorem, the Følner criterion for amenable groups, Fourier uniqueness, and de Bruijn–Erdős compactness. Corollary cor:positive-badness part (i) depends on Gwyn and Stavrianos 2020 (Lemma 2.10 and Theorem 2.11), and part (ii) depends on Bourgeat, Heinrich, Melotti and Robert 2015 (Theorems 1–2) for its needle-frequency bounds. The paper cites Sokolov–Voronov 2025 and Voronov 2025 as precedents for its interface and strip arguments, not as steps it relies on.
event.direction: proves a lower bound: χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6, improving the known lower bound 5
event.object: None for the lower bound. Non-five-colourability is proved by contradiction. The finite unit-distance graph in cor:positive-badness is obtained by compactness and is not displayed. The seven-colouring in the proof of thm:main (hexagonal, from Hadwiger 1961) is explicit, but it is the known upper bound, not a new object.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the exact value of χ(ℝ²). Isbell's ≤7 and de Grey's ≥5 are pre-snapshot bounds (de Grey digested through the alternate proofs, Polymath16 and the journal work built on it). Later re-proofs and smaller 5-chromatic witnesses (Exoo–Ismailescu, Heule, Parts, Voronov, Haugland) leave the quantity where it was, so they are none. Interval, two-distance, fractional, independence-ratio, v_k, sphere and unit-distance-count results answer changed questions, so they are variant. The only after-snapshot event on the problem itself is openai-math-158: it claims χ ≥ 6, which moves the lower bound but does not determine the value, so it is a bound. It is unreviewed, because a Lean build is not digestion (F7). I marked it doubtful rather than credible because it is an unexamined landmark claim whose key steps were only partly read and whose sorry-free status is null; there is no specific error, so it is not knocked down. Its AI role is generated, per the README. The Mundinger ML colourings and the OpenAI unit-distance counterexample are AI-generated but are variants. Codex's LP vertex search in Dúcz–Varga, Gemini running SAT solvers, and Claude's help with the formalisation are tooling or formalisation, so all three are none.
judgement.doubts: openai-math-158 rests on an internal OpenAI repository read in part. Whether the Lean theorem no_proper_five_coloring is sorry-free and faithfully states arbitrary colourings is unverified. If it holds, the lower bound is 6. The Reed May 2026 claim of χ = 7 appears only as a footnote, and the record says it is conditional.
